 By Zachary Small 
 Nov. 4, 2026 Long before the obsession with looksmaxxing and testosterone-boosted biceps, the artist Tom of Finland began to build a cult following in the 1950s around his illustrations of beefy bikers and leather-clad policemen so muscular they practically exploded out of their outfits.
 More than three decades after the artist’s death in 1991, his gay erotica is now held by multiple major museums and featured in fashion shows , films and nightclub bathrooms. The Finnish artist’s former Los Angeles home, the TOM House , is a city landmark and a symbol of the gay community in Echo Park, where it sits.
 But who exactly deserves to guide the legacy of Touko Laaksonen (the artist’s real name) has become the subject of an increasingly bitter dispute between the artist’s former muse, model and business partner, Durk Dehner, and the Tom of Finland Foundation , a nonprofit tasked with protecting the artist’s work.
 Dehner, a Canadian businessman and leatherman , founded the nonprofit with Laaksonen in 1984, and served as president until 2025, when he resigned under pressure from other trustees. Images had resurfaced of him wearing Nazi regalia. Dehner apologized and said they were remnants from an era when some people in fetish communities dressed as Nazis to appear subversive. But he was subsequently dropped as a judge for the pageant International Mr. Leather, with the competition’s executive director saying, “Hate has no place at I.M.L. Period, full stop.”
 Part of the ongoing dispute between Dehner and the foundation concerns money. The trustees say that their review of the foundation’s books found that over the years Dehner received royalty payments for licensing and other fees that they believe were supposed to go to the foundation.
